reconcile.connective: Defenders read Matthew as an abbreviated account: Matthew compresses the scene so the centurion 'approaches' directly, while Luke preserves the elders and friends as intermediaries.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the wording head-on: Matthew has the centurion come and speak in person, whereas Luke says he sent others and never came himself.

skeptic.name: Skeptic's Annotated Bible (Steve Wells)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999– )

excerpts.author: Tyndale
excerpts.excerpt_text: With his tendency to abbreviate accounts, Matthew has the centurion approaching Jesus (Matt 8:5-13). Luke tells the full story in which Jewish elders, and later the centurion’s friends, act as intermediaries.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Resolves the tension by compositional abbreviation: Matthew compresses the account so the centurion 'approaches' directly, while Luke preserves the intermediaries. Squarely answers the wording difference without the weaker 'he probably came at last' move.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the centurion accounts under the harmonizing maxim that what one does through agents is credited to the principal, the same agency reasoning the commentators apply here.

link.title: Matthew 8:5–13 (cf. Luke 7:2–10)—Is there a mistake in the accounts concerning Jesus and the centurion?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment arguing a sent representative spoke as the centurion himself, so Matthew's direct attribution is compatible with Luke's intermediaries.
